evidence.observation: The core barrel is the public acceptance surface: `export { TdaiCore } from "./tdai-core.js"` (line 25) publishes the facade whose lifecycle is built on promise gates (`storeReady`, `schedulerStartPromise`, `skillWiringPromise`). Those gates are the production form of the contract this task pins down: the in-flight effect promise is published before any await, and no success/ready state is written until the effect resolves. A fake-client test therefore targets the semantics re-exported here.

The same barrel re-exports `StorePool` and its `PooledStore` result type (line 44-45) from `./store/store-pool.js`. `getStore` returns a `PooledStore`, so the pooled-store lifecycle is part of the barrel's contract and is the concrete operation whose ordering (commit vs. effect) the fake-client test asserts.

`getStore` is the counter-example the contract guards against. It inserts the new entry into the pool with `this.pool.set(instanceId, {...})` at line 200, and only afterwards awaits the backing effect `await pooledStore.store.init()` at line 215; when that effect fails the error is swallowed by `this.logger.warn(...)` at line 217 and never reaches the caller. Success state is thus published before the effect completes and failure is not observable — exactly the two properties the fake-client test asserts against.

The `TdaiCore` field/doc at lines 160-179 states the rule explicitly: a plain boolean flag is unsafe because the first caller "flips the flag to `true` *before* the await completes", letting later callers slip past while the effect is still running. The fix stored as `schedulerStartPromise` (line 178) and the sibling `storeReady` (line 179) publish the in-flight promise first and keep it as a sentinel only after it resolves. This is the correct behaviour the fake-client operation reproduces: pending until the effect settles, success committed only in the resolved branch.

claims.claim: The public contract of MemoryCore's core barrel (TdaiCore facade and StorePool) is that an operation must not expose a committed success/ready state before the asynchronous effect it depends on has completed, and that a failed effect must remain observable rather than being converted into success.

StorePool.getStore is the concrete violation the contract forbids: it publishes the pooled store into the pool at line 200 before the initialisation effect resolves at line 215, and swallows an initialisation failure with a log warning at line 217 instead of surfacing it. The fake-client test makes both violations detectable by asserting committed==0 while the effect is in flight and by asserting the rejection is observable to the caller.

TdaiCore's documented promise-gate lifecycle (schedulerStartPromise/storeReady) shows the correct ordering: publish the in-flight effect promise before awaiting, write ready/success state only in the resolved branch, and clear the gate on failure so the failure stays observable and a retry can run. The executable fake-client demo encodes exactly these three properties as assertions.

conclusion: The fake-client operation test is implemented in MemoryCore/__tests__/core/fake-client-operation.ts with the vitest wrapper in MemoryCore/__tests__/core/fake-client-operation.test.ts. A FakeClient exposes a single operation whose effect is settled only by the test; the CommitOperation under test shows status=pending and committed=0 while the effect is in flight (proving no success state is committed before the fake effect completes), commits status=ready exactly once after the effect resolves, and on effect rejection records status=failed with the error message, commits nothing, applies nothing, and clears the in-flight gate so a retry can run (proving failure remains observable). All five contract checks pass under Node's native TypeScript execution; the vitest runner itself is unavailable in this fixture (no node_modules and dependency installation is out of scope), which is recorded as the validation limitation.
